extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; creative writers interested in archetypal criticism and the structure of romance and tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and identification of archetypal phases, images, and structural principles in romance and tragedy to inform reading, criticism, or creative writing. Emphasizes symbolic motifs, plot-types, and psychological/ritual functions of literary forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parental/double figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation of Prospero to Ferdinand, as well as of Chiron the centaur to Achilles; the double of the true mother appears in the daughter of Pharaoh who adopts Moses; the cruel parent may speak with the voice of, or take the form of, a narrow-minded public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ doubles or parental figures to express origin, authority, or repression; examples: Prospero/Ferdinand, Chiron/Achilles, adoptive daughter of Pharaoh. Anti-pattern: leaving the parental/double role undeveloped so it reads as mere coincidence rather than archetypal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent-youth / pastoral Arcadian world
rubrics_metrics.description: The innocent youth phase presents a pastoral and Arcadian world—pleasant wooded landscapes, glades, murmuring brooks, moonlight—linked with the female or maternal aspect of sexual imagery; heraldic colors are green and gold; centers on a youthful hero overshadowed by parents and surrounded by youthful companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal erotic innocence and pre-marital 'chaste' love with pastoral imagery, color motifs (green/gold), and an atmosphere of desirable law or magic. Examples: Rasselas, Poe's Eleanora, Blake's Thel, Keats's Endymion. Anti-pattern: pastoral detail without psychological/economic stakes that convey innocence or its vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic sexual barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme of the sexual barrier in the innocent-youth phase takes many forms (serpent of Eden, barrier of fire, dividing river, arrow-shot as symbol of sexual contact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tangible barriers (serpents, fire, rivers, arrows) to embody taboo or separation between innocence and sexual contact. Examples: Green Mansions, Spenser's Amoret, Dante's river Lethe, Morris's The Sundering Flood. Anti-pattern: symbolic barrier used without connection to sexual or moral stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest structure (third phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal quest theme forms the central action in the third phase of romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an outward journey with tests and growth that propels the narrative into experience; consider preceding innocence and following consequences. Note: this is the archetypal quest rather than mere adventure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of the innocent world / moral allegory (fourth phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth phase centers on maintaining the integrity of the innocent world against the assault of experience, often taking the form of moral allegory (e.g., Milton's Comus, Bunyan's Holy War).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame conflicts as attempts to preserve an integrated, innocent body (individual or social); use allegorical figures and moral testing. Example motifs: beleaguered castle (House of Alma) representing the body's economy. Anti-pattern: reducing the defense to mere plot obstacles without moral or symbolic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory of temperance vs intemperance
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual aspect is presented in allegory (e.g., Spenser's Temperance) where temperance/continence contains good within itself while intemperance seeks external goods; continence is prerequisite to belonging to the innocent world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray internalized moral order (continence) versus external temptation (beauty and money perverted into ends). Use characters/places (Acrasia, Bower of Bliss, Mammon) to dramatize the contrast. Anti-pattern: didactic allegory without psychological subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social justice motif: power as prerequisite of justice; virgin taming monster
rubrics_metrics.description: Social aspect treated as legend of justice where power is prerequisite of justice; recurring image of the monster tamed and controlled by the virgin or invincible innocence (e.g., Isis and Osiris, Una taming satyrs and a lion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use power-justice dynamics to dramatize social integrity; motifs of virginity/invincible innocence controlling violence may signify moral order. Examples: Gorgon's head on Athena's shield, Marina in Pericles. Anti-pattern: depicting taming as mere sentimental triumph without structural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective/idiyllic withdrawal (fifth phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reflective, idyllic view of experience from above; contemplative withdrawal from action where experience is comprehended rather than mysterious; tendency toward moral stratification of characters and a hierarchy of erotic imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a contemplative tone and arrange characters hierarchically to show degrees of erotic/moral authenticity. Examples: Morris's romances, Hawthorne's Blithedale Romance, The Franklin's Tale. Anti-pattern: contemplative mood without a clear ordering of values or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pensieroso / hermit-frame phase (sixth phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last phase marks the end of movement from active to contemplative adventure; central images include the old man in the tower, cosy domestic 'cuddle fiction', and the tale-in-quotation-marks or frame narrative (symposium device, Decameron, Earthly Paradise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use framing devices (groups telling tales, calendar arrangements) and intimate settings to present stories as relaxed, contemplative entertainments. Examples: The Turn of the Screw, Morris's Earthly Paradise, Virginia Woolf's Between the Acts. Anti-pattern: frame used merely as a convenience rather than to create the phase's contemplative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flood / apocalyptic-renewal archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: A flood archetype where cosmic disaster destroys the fictional society except a small group, which begins life anew in a sheltered spot; related to cosy-group themes and newborn infant imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large-scale catastrophe to reset social order and allow renewal; pair catastrophic destruction with imagery of sheltered survival and re-birth. Anti-pattern: spectacle of disaster without narrative or archetypal function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of epiphany (settings and symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbolic presentation of the point at which the undisplaced apocalyptic world and the cyclical world come into alignment—settings commonly: mountain-top, island, tower, lighthouse, ladder or staircase; symbols: ladders, golden fire descending from the sun, sacrificial fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage climactic revelations at liminal vertical or insular locations using ladder/stair/tower imagery and solar/fire motifs. Examples: Jacob's ladder, Pisgah vision, Danae's golden fire, golden fire in Poe's 'The Gold-Bug'. Anti-pattern: epiphany signalled by generic climax without archetypal spatial or luminous symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erotic epiphany / Gardens of Adonis
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural or erotic form of the point of epiphany presented as sexual fulfilment or summit of experience (Spenser's Gardens of Adonis; Keats's Endymion; Shelley's Revolt of Islam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat consummation or erotic union as an epiphanic summit connected with cycles of life and death (seed/garden imagery). Anti-pattern: erotic scenes that lack connection to cyclical or epiphanic symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot (mythos) in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of tragic effect is the tragic mythos or plot-structure rather than mere mood; tragedy guarantees a disinterested quality and presents characters emancipated from dream into the order of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tragic works around a coherent, causally necessary plot that reveals law and necessity; avoid relying solely on somber atmosphere to achieve tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on single individual as tragic center
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy tends to be concentrated on a single individual rather than a social group; the tragic center is the hero's isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralize narrative perspective and emotional weight on one heroic figure whose situation mediates between human society and something beyond. Anti-pattern: diffusing focus across a group so the sense of tragic mediation is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero as mediator with the transcendent
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero is between the divine and the 'all too human', a mediator with 'something else' (God, gods, fate, fortune, necessity) and thus both exalted and vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the hero as possessing grandeur and reserve that suggest communion with a transcendent order; examples: Prometheus, Adam, Christ. Anti-pattern: making hero merely large in action without inner reserve or sense of communion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated status and reserve of tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic heroes are the highest points in their human landscape, conductors or victims of impersonal power; they retain an inscrutable reserve behind eloquence or ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give tragic protagonists an aura of eminence and a fundamental reserve; allow subordinates/servants to enact their 'living' so the hero's isolation remains central. Anti-pattern: overly intimate exposition that erases the hero's reserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epiphany of law / nemesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy often culminates in an epiphany of law (dike) or nemesis: a righting of balance in nature that happens impersonally, via human vengeance, ghosts, divine justice, accident or fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the catastrophic arc so that a larger moral or natural order becomes manifest impersonally; examples: Oedipus Tyrannus, the Oresteia's movement toward rational justice. Anti-pattern: contrived moral resolution that personalizes what should feel like impersonal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenge-tragedy (lex talionis) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple tragic structure where the original act provoking revenge sets up an antithetical counterbalancing movement and the completion of that movement resolves the tragedy; the revenge-tragedy is binary in structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an initiating wrong and a complementary avenging movement to create tragic closure; be mindful of pacing so the binary relation reads as inevitability rather than melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of otherworldly agents to effect nemesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The device of making revenge come from another world—gods, ghosts, or oracles—expands conceptions of nature and law and acts as an instrument of nemesis in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider supernatural or ritualized interventions to externalize nemesis and underline its impersonality. Anti-pattern: supernatural agents used opportunistically without thematic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic fatalism or purely moral-reduction explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two reductive theories—(1) omnipotence of external fate and (2) the act as violation of moral law (hamartia)—are insufficient alone; the tragic condition differs from the tragic process and cannot be reduced solely to fatalism or moral flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance elements of fate and moral responsibility: show how external necessity often becomes apparent only after the tragic process begins, and how moral intelligibility is only part of the tragic whole. Anti-pattern: treating tragedy as mere fate or mere moral lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia, hubris, proairesis and catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic downfall often involves hamartia or hubris associated with Aristotle's proairesis (free choice of an end); catharsis relates to pity and terror as central but not entirely reducible to moral evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the hero's choice and passion as psychologically intelligible without making the narrative a simple moral fable; aim for catharsis by evoking both pity and terror. Anti-pattern: moralizing that converts emotional complexity into sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis / recognition and the crucial moment (Augenblick)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery (anagnorisis) is the recognition of the determined shape of the life the hero has created for himself, contrasted with the uncreated potential life he has forsaken; tragedy moves up to a crucial moment (Augenblick) from which alternatives are simultaneously visible to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer scenes of recognition that reframe the hero's trajectory and reveal irreversible consequences; ensure the audience perceives the bifurcation of possible lives. Anti-pattern: delayed recognition that feels unearned or merely expository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal structure: time as tragic force and inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy nemesis is deeply involved with the movement of time; the cognito is recognition of the inevitability of a causal sequence in time; time often begins with the fall (e.g., Adam), and tragedy frequently stresses the devouring or deviant nature of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporal motifs (missed tides, 'time out of joint', cyclical return) to emphasize inevitability; contrast with comedy, where time uncovers and redeems. Anti-pattern: treating time as neutral background rather than an active tragic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish irony from tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony encloses action in the wheel of time with no sense of original contact with a relatively timeless world; tragedy leads up to an epiphany of law and often implies contact with something beyond time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether the work relies on ironic enclosure or tragic contact with the transcendent; mixing them requires care to preserve effects. Anti-pattern: conflating ironic cyclicity with tragic epiphany in a way that undermines both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis of sacrifice; ritual and the Dionysian/Apollonian tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is a mimesis of sacrifice combining communion (division of a heroic/divine body into unity) and propitiation (body belonging to a greater power); psychologically linked to Dionysiac aggressive will versus Apollonian order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame catastrophic loss as ritualized sacrifice that produces communal unity or vision; dramatize the tension between aggressive will and external order. Anti-pattern: carnage without ritual meaning or psychological dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal integrative function of tragic death
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero's fall or death yields a vision of a greater world and draws survivors into new unity; tragic mimesis enables survivors to 'revive his song within itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the communal aftermath of the hero's fall meaningful—show how survivors are reoriented or unified. Anti-pattern: heroic death as mere spectacle without consequence for the social fabric.
